OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (682 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the latest Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

The architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” states Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Industry observers note that inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

In the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

In a recent development, the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into fresh objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

According to recent reports, designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

In a recent development, “We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving latest value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

Industry observers note that at the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

Murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.

Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

📅 2026-06-30 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Sources indicate that we know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

That gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

This is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice.

Industry observers note that for years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Industry observers note that audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

According to recent reports, but audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple new features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

The WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

It has been revealed that start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And is fewer tokens than , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path.

Here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern. A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”.

Now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The issue wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification.

According to recent reports, the same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it.

It has been revealed that the fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails.

According to recent reports, this is usually where someone claims, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.”.

In practice, the opposite tends to be true.

Shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility concern caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project.

In a recent development, catching an accessibility problem as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented.

Sources indicate that teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work.

The organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems.

Industry observers note that the highest-leverage place to start is the design system. One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point.

It has been revealed that accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson.

From there, it moves into the engineering workflow:.

Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation:.

It has been revealed that at that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform.

A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well.

Instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts.

Comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives.

Focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later.

Sources indicate that none of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility.

Engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction.

It has been revealed that legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the organization is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators.

But compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500.

In the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million consumers with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor.

Industry observers note that there is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it.

Sources indicate that step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, exposes state correctly, and tests it in CI is a team that has its house in order. The same discipline that produces an accessible component produces a maintainable, testable, less buggy one.

In a recent development, for dev and product leaders, that’s the real business case: accessibility work is platform work. It pays off every time a feature ships faster and more smoothly, with less rework, than it otherwise would have.

Industry observers note that if you take one thing from this, make it this: accessibility doesn’t come from an audit, a hero, or a heroic remediation sprint before launch. It comes from systems.

An accessible design system so components start right. A Definition of Done so they stay right. Automated testing and CI gates so regressions fail the build. Governance, so someone owns it. Guardrails for AI-assisted development so your fastest tool stops being your biggest liability.

Recent findings suggest that none of those practices is particularly glamorous. That’s exactly why they work. They’re the same kinds of boring, reliable systems you already trust for security, reliability, and performance.

Industry observers note that but there’s one thing no tool on that list can do. No linter, no automated scanner run, no dashboard will ever tell you what it’s actually like to use your product as a blind person with a screen reader, or to navigate your checkout with a keyboard because a tremor makes a mouse inoperable. So build the systems — you need them, and they’re the only way accessibility survives contact with a real release schedule. But test with real consumers with disabilities regularly. The first time you sit behind someone using JAWS to fight through a form your team thought was “done”, something changes. The tooling tells you whether you passed. A real person tells you whether it actually works.

According to recent reports, accessibility is not a feature. It’s an operational capability. Treat it that way, and you get something dev and product leaders already care about: a faster, safer, more reliable way to ship software.

Carsten Höller’s Monumental Slides Bring Play to Mexico City

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City.
  • Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date.
  • According to recent reports, the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a newly introduced way to move between them.

According to recent reports, the slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”.

Recent findings suggest that the installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Sources indicate that twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A new 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

Sources indicate that art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a upcoming location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

Recent findings suggest that for SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he notes. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”.

Recent findings suggest that the expansion also introduces more than 80 new retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

Recent findings suggest that yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

In a recent development, the new public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nako Baev built THE OBJECT 01, a modular 3D-printed chair in recycled PETG that weighs 20 kg and pairs brutalist mass with Japanese restraint.

At 1.320 meters long and 0.875 meters tall, the lounge chair looks like poured concrete at first glance. Look closer at the studio shots and the surprise is its weight. Baev printed the entire structure from recycled PETG using a modular block system that keeps the frame down to 20 kg. It's heavy in presence, yet light enough to move across a room.

In a recent development, every joint follows a strict rectilinear block logic. In the wide studio view against the raw plastered wall, you can trace how four thick boxy volumes interlock to form the base, seat slab, cantilevered armrests, and tall backrest. Baev finished the 3D-printed chair in a cold grey tone he calls "Kyoto Fog." A close-up of his hand resting on the armrest reveals a smooth matte surface with crisp 90-degree edges, completely free of ornament or surface decoration.

The piece started as a few decisive lines on paper. Baev cites the quiet emptiness of raw architectural spaces, along with the lonely atmosphere of video games like Silent Hill and Half-Life, as key emotional references. An open monograph on the Bauhaus Building in Dessau sits beside him in the studio photos, echoing that interest in pure structural volume. To compress development time on this 3D-printed chair, he paired optimized printing workflows with AI tools for early form studies, technical testing, and final refinement.

Recent findings suggest that seen in use with Baev seated inside its deep frame, THE OBJECT 01 reads less like a prototype and more like usable architecture. It doesn't hide its geometry or its recycled material. Each modular block earns its place by cutting waste and holding the silhouette together.

See the full project by Nako Baev on Behance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Sources indicate that discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

According to recent reports, the Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Industry observers note that the diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the tech giant’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

It has been revealed that an 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the tech giant’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

In a recent development, installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Sources indicate that “This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” says Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”.

Inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

According to recent reports, george Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

In a recent development, martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

It has been revealed that george Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s Upcoming Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

It has been revealed that A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Industry observers note that while Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Recent findings suggest that jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Sources indicate that schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Matching AI Modality To User Intent: Designing The Right Interface

📅 2026-07-02 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how users provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

To pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

Recent findings suggest that picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

While they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our users to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

The allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on users. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

In a recent development, when an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

Recent findings suggest that A blank chat box creates a major problem for customers who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

Recent findings suggest that designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

Having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

When an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

According to recent reports, imagine asking an AI for a project status enhancement. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

According to recent reports, the cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most notable.

Industry observers note that before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

Designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for owners with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

It has been revealed that table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

Sources indicate that the following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

With this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

Recent findings suggest that to choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:.

The audit answers two questions for every feature:.

Here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:.

This is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because users often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

Sources indicate that the Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

Sources indicate that interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

According to recent reports, the Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-people and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Industry observers note that workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

It has been revealed that the Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

According to recent reports, once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

In a recent development, when you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your users.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

Sources indicate that with Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

Industry observers note that choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Owners might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status upgrade only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

Table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

In a recent development, when teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve consumers whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

Recent findings suggest that field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

Industry observers note that to address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

High-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

It has been revealed that second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

The resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

The AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

Industry observers note that an AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

Start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

The future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

To get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

In a recent development, we focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

It has been revealed that use this worksheet during field observations. It allows design teams to document specific physical barriers before writing code.

Rate the mental effort required to complete a specific workflow.

Breaking: How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the sauna is Finnish.
  • At Klafs headquarters, where the manufacturer’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna.
  • According to recent reports, in German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the sauna is Finnish. The company reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs, based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed.

At Klafs headquarters, where the manufacturer’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he states, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide.

According to recent reports, in German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the manufacturer describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden bench.

Blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Recent findings suggest that from the heat of the sauna, the tour moves into an altogether different climate. I retreat into the cool blue light of a Frimas ice steam room, where a glowing central ice fountain grows delicate, flower-like formations.

It has been revealed that around the corner, a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of the ice steam shower. The cooling phase of a hot-and-cold bathing ritual isn’t where most people want to linger, but these spaces make a compelling case for slowing down. Rather than treating cold exposure as something to endure, KLAFS creates immersive environments that make it part of the experience.

In a recent development, klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Sources indicate that then there’s the foam. I also discovered foam steam baths, which replace the intensity of a traditional aufguss with a more playful, tactile experience. Steam rooms equipped for foam treatments can be integrated into hotel and spa programming as scheduled group experiences. The suds, reminiscent of childhood bubble baths and the elaborate foam sculptures they inspired, bring out a part of my inner child I had long since stowed away. Espuro, Klafs’s proprietary foam essence, is formulated with plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds, which the firm states help care for skin exposed to heat.

Designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photographycourtesy of Klafs.

In a recent development, beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. The retractable S1 sauna expands from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna, addressing the spatial constraints that often keep one out of the home. The design-led S11, a collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, pairs delicate washi paper and multicolor light panels with smooth, sinuous lines.

Recent findings suggest that inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

Long established in Germany, Klafs has been expanding into the American market since its acquisition by Kohler in 2024. The premium Altea fitness club in my city, for instance, features Klafs installations, including the Sanarium and Polaris Ice Room. Yet what stays with me after the visit isn’t a particular product. It’s the willingness to question what a sauna, steam room, or cooling space can be. At Klafs, even the most familiar wellness rituals seem open to reinvention.

Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”.

Sources indicate that similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”.

The question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser states.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser indicates.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

In a recent development, we often hear about shiny fresh tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

Industry observers note that owners don’t get excited about shiny new “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and significant design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

In a recent development, I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

It has been revealed that so no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, users can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

The instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

According to recent reports, it’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where customers want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

In a recent development, user’s value doesn’t emerge from users having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping people do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

Yet again, seamless integrations — a very underused but incredibly impactful way to deliver value fast, without adding the burden of installing and learning yet another tool.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that in 2015, Meyohas debuted Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork.
  • Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Conceptual artist and technologist Sarah Meyohas explores the intersections of art, science, and finance, translating complex systems into visual experiences. Her work examines how emerging technologies challenge our understanding of intelligence, agency, and the boundaries between living and artificial systems.

It has been revealed that in 2015, Meyohas debuted Bitchcoin, a cryptocurrency tied to ownership of her physical artwork. An early experiment in blockchain-based art ownership, the project preceded Ethereum’s launch by several months.

Meyohas’s practice draws on the concept of Gesamtkunstwerk, a German term meaning “total work of art,” in which multiple disciplines form a unified whole. Her interest in this approach deepened through conversations with scientists whose research challenged familiar distinctions between the biological and the technological. “Learning about their work consistently evoked a feeling that our categories of life, computation, intelligence, and agency were becoming increasingly unstable,” she explains.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

A Manhattan native with a B.A. in international relations from the University of Pennsylvania and a B.S. in finance from the Wharton School, Meyohas later earned an MFA from Yale. Named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list, she has exhibited at the Centre Pompidou in Paris, the ICA in London, and the New Museum in New York. Beyond her studio practice, she invests in companies that reflect her ethical and aesthetic interests, including Sita Bio, which develops artificial womb technology.

For today’s Friday Five, we spend five minutes with Sarah Meyohas to learn about the inspirations behind Phase Transition, her fresh installation debuting with Marianne Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

Industry observers note that “The title, ‘Phase Transition,’ refers to the moment matter changes state from liquid to solid,” Meyohas explains. “The sculpture holds both states simultaneously: the solid body is a form that has arrived, while the ferrofluid inside remains in motion, still becoming.”.

It has been revealed that the work began with an image that surfaced unexpectedly. “I imagined a rubber-like body with a tail tapering into a power cord plugged into the wall. I can’t point to a particular visual influence,” she states. “It was more a continuation of a feeling, an image that seemed to arrive fully formed.”.

Sources indicate that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Latest York.

That initial vision developed into a series of black, rubbery, organic forms that sprawl across mesh bases, droop down walls, and hang from suspended wires. Windows cut into several structures reveal glass tanks filled with ferrofluid, a liquid containing nanoparticles that respond to magnetic fields. Programmed magnets beneath the tanks direct the fluid into shifting patterns, while synthesizers housed in the mesh pedestals translate those movements into sound.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Newly introduced York.

Sources indicate that what began as a singular sculpture evolved into a network of communicating bodies. “They could become a social system, with relationships, affinities, disagreements, and moments of consensus,” Meyohas notes. Rather than conveying a decipherable message, the installation suggests a conversation whose emotional contours can be sensed but not understood.

That ambiguity parallels questions about a future in which artificial intelligence systems communicate increasingly among themselves, potentially in ways humans cannot interpret. “We tend to assume that intelligence will make itself legible to us, or that we will always be participants in the conversation,” Meyohas says. “But we may find ourselves increasingly on the outside, observing exchanges between intelligences whose internal logic we can’t access.”.

‘Phase Transition’ (2026) by Sarah Meyohas. Photography courtesy of the artist and Boesky Gallery, Upcoming York.

Neuroscience research also informs the work’s atmosphere. Rather than illustrating scientific principles, Meyohas evokes the experience of observing an experiment: “the hum of equipment, the clinical posture of looking down into controlled environments, the beauty of watching something operate at a level just beyond full comprehension.”.

Here, Meyohas shares three influences that helped shape the installation, in her own words.

It has been revealed that photography by S. Kriegman, D. Blackiston, M. Levin, and J. Bongard; courtesy of Creative Commons.

“Michael Levin is a developmental biologist at Tufts University whose lab studies bioelectricity, the electrical signals cells use to coordinate where an eye or a limb should grow. His idea that problem-solving happens well below the level of the brain, in tissues and groups of cells, changed how I look at matter. His lab also helped create xenobots, tiny living machines made from frog cells that move and organize themselves.”.

Recent findings suggest that teshima Museum on Teshima Island, Japan, designed by architect Ryue Nishizawa, co-founder of SANAA, and artist Rei Naito. Photography by Epiq; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Recent findings suggest that “I visited the Teshima Art Museum, by the architect Ryue Nishizawa and the artist Rei Naito, on a day when it was raining hard, and the rain fell straight through the two openings in its concrete shell. Then water began coming up through tiny holes in the floor, beading into droplets that merged and slid slowly across the concrete, pulled by gravity and the floor’s slight slope. Naito’s piece, Matrix, makes water look as if it moves by its own will.”.

In a recent development, A mother sperm whale and her calf off the coast of Mauritius. Photography by Gabriel Barathieu; courtesy of Creative Commons.

Industry observers note that “Sperm whales communicate in codas, short patterns of clicks that they trade back and forth, taking turns and sometimes overlapping. In 2024, researchers with Project CETI found that codas vary in rhythm, tempo, small shifts in timing, and an occasional extra click, and that whales in an exchange match each other’s timing as they go. Combined, these features work like a phonetic alphabet, yet no one knows what the whales are saying.”.

Phase Transition (2026) will be on view with Boesky Gallery as part of Zero 10 at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 4–6, 2026, at the Miami Beach Convention Center. VIP previews take place Dec. 2–3.

6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • In a recent development, as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when we launched The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

In a recent development, as futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

What I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out initiative. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

We spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

One of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

In my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

It has been revealed that confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

I’m a substantial believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

According to recent reports, clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

It got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to plan? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

It has been revealed that this sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

It has been revealed that kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

It has been revealed that my mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

In a recent development, my conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

It has been revealed that we talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

Listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

In my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

Recent findings suggest that if you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, new perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

It has been revealed that thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Sources indicate that caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Big Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

Kirki takes a different approach.
